sections.h2: Where Williams County deeds get filed
sections.html:
Head to the second floor of the courthouse, One Courthouse Square, Bryan, OH 43506, or call 419-636-3259. The counter operates on weekdays from 8:30 a.m. until 4:30 p.m. Filings must arrive by 4:00 p.m.

Staff keep a lasting record of every paper that transfers or encumbers land, and indexing lets a searcher follow who held title and which debts attach. Bryan is the county seat and the biggest city.

Senate Bill 94 let counties add a $5.00 preservation surcharge under R.C. 317.32, and the Williams County Recorder has applied it since January 1, 2025. Reference fees and the standardization guidelines still apply on top.

Williams County Recorder charges
Document or serviceAmount
Recording, pages one and two$39.00
Each page after two$8.00
Reference fee$4.00
Paper that misses the format rules$20.00 added
Copy made at the counter$0.25 per page
Copy ordered in writing$2.00 per page

Certified copies follow the Ohio Revised Code schedule on the Recorder's fees page.

R.C. 317.114 gives every recorder the same standard so that recording stamps have room on the page. A deed that falls short is still recorded, with $20 more collected. Williams County's Recorder asks for the following.

  • Dark blue or black ink only, and no highlighter.
  • A font of 10 points or larger.
  • One inch of white space left, right and bottom.
  • Page one keeps 3 inches clear at the top, later pages 1.5 inches.
  • Paper from letter size (8.5 by 11) to legal length (8.5 by 14).

Four categories escape the rules: documents signed before July 1, 2009, papers from a court or taxing authority, state and federal forms with DD214 discharges, and plats.

A conveyance can arrive by mail only after the Engineer and the Auditor have stamped it, a rule that covers deeds, land contracts, easements and affidavits. The County Engineer reviews the legal description, the Auditor then names the conveyance charge, and for many documents the Treasurer first confirms that taxes on the parcel are paid.

  • Engineer: clears the legal description.
  • Treasurer: validates payment of taxes.
  • Auditor, 419-636-5639: states the charge.
  • Recorder: records and indexes the stamped deed.

The Auditor's conveyance fee is $4 per $1,000 of price, with a transfer fee of $0.50 per parcel or deed. R.C. 319.202 assigns that fee to the grantor and requires the grantee's value statement. New conveyance standards started on January 1, 2026, and a link to them is on the Auditor's page.

The July 2025 population estimate is 36,549, a 1.5 percent drop from the April 2020 base. Of 16,659 housing units, 76.3 percent have owner occupants. The middle owner-held home is worth $150,000, and middle gross rent is $791. Only 44 building permits were pulled in 2025, so resale homes make up most of what is on the market.

Many sales here involve farm lots and older homes in small towns, which means legal descriptions deserve a careful look. An older deed may describe a parcel by metes and bounds, and the Engineer's review is where mismatches surface. Raise any boundary question with your title company well before closing, not at the counter on the day you file.

sections.h2: Getting a copy of a deed
sections.html:
Walk in, and the counter copy of a public record, a deed among them, is $0.25 per page, with staff glad to help find it. Written requests run $2.00 per page and need the volume and page from the Ohio Land Records index, a check or money order, and a stamped envelope addressed to you. Phone and email requests are not filled.

That online index covers filings from October 25, 1999 forward and shows new entries within a day of recording. It names the owner, document type and property description without displaying the document itself. Certified copies exist, though in person a plain copy costs the same $0.25 per page, so request a certified one only when a lender or court insists on it.

Plats are searchable through the County Engineer's site. The Recorder holds records back to the start of land ownership in the county, and because the online index begins in 1999, older deeds need a trip to the courthouse.

Watch for a mailer called a "Deed Processing Notice" from a South Dakota company that asks homeowners for $83 to send a deed copy. Deeds are public records, so a friend can collect one for you at the courthouse.

Before you order a copy, write down the owner's name and the approximate filing date so you can find the volume and page in the index quickly. If the deed predates the online index, tell the clerk the parcel number and the names of earlier owners, and staff can point you to the right book.

sections.h2: Other courthouse offices that touch a sale
sections.html:
The county's Useful Links page maps the neighbors of the Recorder.

  • Probate Court: estates, guardianships and trusts, relevant when a house passes through an estate before sale.
  • Planning Commission handles zoning questions about lots and uses.
  • Records Center is the county repository for both public and confidential county records.
  • Clerk of Courts takes passports, divorce records and common pleas cases.
  • Property Fraud Alert: guidance for owners who worry about forged filings.

The Auditor, Engineer and Treasurer sit alongside these offices on the same courthouse square, and the Recorder is the last stop for a deed.

sections.h2: Steps from signed deed to recorded deed
sections.html:
A seller's route through the courthouse goes like this.

  • Have an attorney or title company draft the deed to the layout rules above.
  • Take the legal description to the Engineer for review.
  • Ask the Treasurer to confirm the parcel's taxes are paid.
  • Pay the conveyance fee at the Auditor and get the stamp.
  • File with the Recorder before 4:00 p.m., with the right fee.

A cash sale skips the lender's paperwork, but the stamps and the recording fee stay the same. If an inherited house is involved, check with the Probate Court first so the deed comes from the right party. Call 419-636-3259 if you are unsure what a particular paper needs.

Keep the recorded deed and the receipt once you have them. Your buyer's lender may ask for proof of recording, and so may you if a later tax or title question comes up. If anything was refused at the counter, the clerk can tell you which stamp or correction is missing so you can fix it and return the same day.

faqs.q: What time does the Williams County Recorder stop taking deeds?
faqs.a: At 4:00 p.m., half an hour before the office closes. The counter is upstairs in the Bryan courthouse and opens at 8:30 a.m. on weekdays.

faqs.q: What will recording one Williams County deed cost?
faqs.a: Expect $39.00 for a deed of up to two pages, then $8.00 for every page beyond that. Reference fees of $4.00 may be added, and sloppy formatting brings a $20.00 penalty.

faqs.q: How is the Williams County conveyance fee figured?
faqs.a: The Auditor charges $4 per $1,000 of the purchase price, with $0.50 for each parcel or deed as the transfer fee. Ask the Auditor for the total on your price.

faqs.q: Does the Williams County Recorder accept deeds by mail?
faqs.a: Only when the Engineer and the Auditor have stamped the document beforehand. The same goes for land contracts, easements and affidavits.

faqs.q: What is the cheapest way to get my Williams County deed copy?
faqs.a: Stop by the Recorder's counter, where copies are a quarter a page. A mailed request costs $2.00 per page and must give the volume and page, with payment and a self addressed envelope.
